atlanta-made-the-east-work.title: Atlanta made the East leaders earn it
sections: Before Charlotte ever got to Miami, Atlanta had a vote. The Kings took three of four from the Hurricanes and split two with Charlotte, opening the latter set with a 9–3 win. Miami entered its showdown five and a half back. Atlanta mattered to that margin even though it finished August 30 ten games out.

The Kings swept the closing set with Tampa Bay, including a 14-inning 8–6 win. Eric Gray had five hits in the 10–0 opener, and Jordan Santistevan drove in three runs in each of the first two. Across the ten games Atlanta outscored the opposition 61–28. It took a good stretch against the leaders and turned it into an 8–2 challenge.
Dallas gets the Kings next. The Rustlers have a one-game lead over idle Chicago on August 31. Atlanta’s first outside assignment gives it another chance to leave its mark on somebody else’s race.

august-31-division-and-wild-card-board.title: Six division races and two wild cards after the August challenge
sections: The August Division Challenges added 121 verified finals, including the completion of the previously unfinished St. Louis–Houston game. The regular-season ledger now has 1,571 finals through August 30. St. Louis led the window at 9–2. Atlanta and Philadelphia went 8–2. Detroit, Tampa Bay and New York each went 1–9.
Below, the first record is through August 19, the second through August 30. The bracketed record covers August 20–30. Games back compares each club with the leader at the same cutoff.

Miami swept Charlotte and reduced the margin from four and a half games to one and a half. Atlanta won three of four from Miami, split with Charlotte and swept Tampa Bay. Miami visits Phoenix beginning August 31, Charlotte hosts Chicago beginning September 1, and the Hurricanes get four more directly against Charlotte there September 24–27.

Phoenix broke the August 19 tie by taking three of four at San Francisco. The Warriors’ three wins in four against Los Angeles kept them a game back. The Cobras are still two back despite sweeping San Diego and going 6–4 overall. Each pair of the top three still meets. San Francisco visits Los Angeles September 24–27 and hosts Phoenix September 28–30. Phoenix also has six with Los Angeles, including four to finish the schedule.

Houston kept an eight-game lead by winning its final two against Nashville. The Blues split with all three division opponents. Las Vegas’s lead over Denver shrank from three to one, and its advantage over Seattle from five to one. Seattle won three of four against Las Vegas and tied the Gamblers before the last day. Denver won both games against Las Vegas, then won the last two at Seattle to pull even with the Comets. Portland took three of four at Denver and split four with Las Vegas. All three contenders play one another again by October 4.
Wild cards and the DCS under the 1981 rules

Each conference sends three division winners and its best remaining club. Miami is 71–59, half a game ahead of Chicago (71–60), two and a half ahead of San Francisco (69–62), three and a half ahead of Los Angeles (68–63), and five and a half ahead of Detroit (66–65). Detroit held the wild-card position on August 19.

Denver and Seattle are tied at 71–60 in the ABC, four games in front of both Cincinnati and St. Louis and six ahead of Philadelphia. Denver held the wild-card position alone on August 19. The standings supply no official decision between Denver and Seattle.

If the season ended on these records, Charlotte would be the NBC’s top seed and Miami its wild card. The same-division protection would pair Charlotte with Phoenix and Dallas with Miami. In the ABC, Houston would face the Denver–Seattle wild-card survivor, with Las Vegas facing Boston. The August standings establish position. The remaining schedule and any official tiebreak determine the field.
Roster expansion and September assignments

Twenty-two clubs have 31 games listed. Miami and Minneapolis have 32. Eight games are scheduled for August 31. Miami at Phoenix crosses a wild-card leader with a division leader, Detroit at San Francisco brings two NBC chasers together, and Pittsburgh at Denver and Nashville at Seattle give the tied ABC wild-card clubs separate tests. Dallas can gain half a game on idle Chicago by beating Atlanta.

The August 20 briefing asked how deadline arrivals would be used. Miami’s Addie de Ruijter drove in 12 runs during the challenge, including all four in the Charlotte opener. Justin Bowen, acquired from Boston, saved four games for Chicago. Those are two different ways the deadline deals are showing up in the race. Keep their actual use in view when the active lists get longer.

The league export schedules active rosters to expand from 26 to 40 on September 1. Expansion is still marked inactive at this cutoff. boston-galvez-bought-room.title: Jorge Galvez gave Boston room to breathe
sections: Philadelphia came to Boston for four with a four-game deficit. The Patriots shut the Fury out twice, then lost the next two by a combined 18–4. The split sent the Fury away still four back. Boston kept three of those games in hand even after Philadelphia ran its winning streak to eight.

Jorge Galvez allowed one earned run in 24⅓ innings during the challenge. On August 30 in Pittsburgh he gave up five hits over nine innings and Boston needed only two runs. Mike Randolph recorded six saves in the challenge. The finale showed that Boston could finish a series without calling on him.

Boston won seven of ten and starts September at Houston. The Fury return to Boston on September 28. The Patriots have several road series before then in which to protect the margin their pitchers helped keep.

charlotte-lead-after-miami.title: Charlotte’s lead survived four close losses
sections: Six runs separated Charlotte from Miami across four games. The Colonels lost 4–2, 4–3, 5–3 and 6–5. On August 30 they had the game tied in the bottom of the ninth before Pat Watters ended it with a single. The 1980 division winner heads home still first, with its lead down to a game and a half.

Tampa Bay and Atlanta explain why Charlotte still has that lead. The Colonels won four of their first six, adding a game to their August 19 margin before the sweep. In Miami, Dabir Aly struck out ten in the opener and the Colonels scored twice. Miguel Salazar had 17 hits over the full challenge. There was individual production on a trip where four short scores in succession mattered more.

Charlotte opens September at home against Chicago, itself a game out in the Central. Miami comes to Charlotte for four September 24–27. Those dates put the advantage back in the Colonels’ hands if they can carry a lead to the rematch.

chicago-earned-the-right-to-chase.title: Chicago earned the right to chase Dallas
sections: The August 20 Observer conversation gave Chicago credit for a plus-27 run differential in the Conference Challenges and asked when it would show in the standings. This time seven wins came with a much smaller surplus, 40 runs to 34. Heriberto Jimenez gave the Fire eight scoreless innings and 13 strikeouts in their 1–0 opening victory over Detroit. Chicago won both games on August 21 and took three of four from the Dukes.

The Fire split with Dallas and lost a 14-inning game at Minneapolis on Hirotoshi Nishimoto’s sacrifice fly. They took the other three games from the Blizzard. Those are the wins that mattered while Dallas was sweeping Detroit. Last year Chicago won this division and Detroit went on to win the Grand Series. Chicago now has to find a way past Dallas or Miami.

The Fire start September at Charlotte. Playing the East leader while Miami opens in Phoenix tests both of Chicago’s routes. Dallas remains on the schedule six times, four of them on the final weekend.

sections: Dallas opened the challenge with 17 runs at Minneapolis and lost the next three there. It split two games in Chicago and was level with the Fire when Detroit arrived. The Rustlers’ four-game sweep of the defending champions was emphatic, by a combined 20–4. The reward in the standings was a one-game lead, with Chicago still close enough to make the next Dallas loss count.

Anton Garay allowed four hits over eight scoreless innings against Detroit on August 29. He had already given Dallas eight scoreless innings in Minneapolis with no decision, in a game the Rustlers lost 1–0 in ten. The two starts tell the difference between getting a good outing and turning it into an August result.
Dallas opens at home against Atlanta, an 8–2 club in the challenge. Six games remain against the Fire. Two are in Chicago in September, and the final four of the season are in Dallas.

Tony Oubre went eight innings in the 4–2 win. Damian Serano struck out seven in 5⅔ innings in the 2–1 finale. Denver came home level with Seattle and one game behind Las Vegas. The 5–5 record matters less than the clubs Denver took those four late decisions from.

sections: Detroit scored 11 in its only win of the challenge and four runs in four games at Dallas. The 11–3 win in Chicago came after two August 21 losses. Minneapolis then won twice in Detroit before the Dukes went to Dallas. A team that had begun the challenge one game out ended it six back.

Alex Diaz had 14 hits and six walks over the ten games. Against Dallas, Detroit never scored more than two in a game. Both facts are worth carrying into September. A productive line from one hitter did not turn those four games, and the champions also lost their place at the top of the wild-card standings.

Detroit opens at San Francisco, a club two places ahead of it on the wild-card line behind Miami, with Los Angeles also between them. The next stop is Charlotte. Both opponents have races of their own to protect, and Detroit needs to start taking decisions from teams in front of it.

houston-eight-game-buffer.title: Houston still has eight games to spend
sections: Houston lost twice to St. Louis on August 20, on different fields. First came the 5–3 completion of the unfinished game in Houston, then a 7–1 loss in St. Louis to open the regular four-game set. Houston lost those four by a combined 32–3. A stretch that began with the league’s best record ended with eight losses in 11 games.

There were ways for Houston to win even in that stretch. Scott Szell allowed three earned runs in 25 innings across three starts. The Mavericks beat Cincinnati 3–2 in 16 innings, and their bats recovered for 10–0 and 10–9 wins to finish against Nashville. Apostolos Georghiou homered and had three hits in the last game. Houston still leads Cincinnati and St. Louis by eight.
Boston and Denver come to Houston to start September. The East leader and one of the two clubs tied for the wild card give Houston an early look at the company it may have in October.

miami-makes-four-count.title: Miami made all four count
sections: The last out of the Charlotte series never came. Pat Watters singled with two gone in the ninth, Dwayne Postell scored, and Miami won its fourth straight game against the division leader. On August 20 the question was whether Miami could get close enough that four wins would give it first. Six games later the answer was still no. The Hurricanes needed those four just to get within a game and a half.

Atlanta took three of the opening four. Two Miami wins over Tampa Bay followed, by 10–3 and 9–1. Then Addie de Ruijter, acquired from Phoenix on July 29, drove in all four runs in the first game against Charlotte. The newcomers were part of the August 20 question. De Ruijter gave Miami a concrete answer in a game with a direct bearing on first place.

Miami now owns the NBC wild-card lead by half a game over Chicago. At 71 wins it is within two of its entire 1980 total. Its next series is in Phoenix, where de Ruijter’s former club leads the West. The return series with Charlotte begins September 24 on the Colonels’ field.

one-game-is-the-new-margin.title: The contenders can hear each other now
sections: Two outs in the ninth, a tie score, and Pat Watters had a one-and-two count. He singled to left, Dwayne Postell scored, and Miami won 6–5. Charlotte had come to Miami with five and a half games to spare. It left with a game and a half. The Colonels are still first in the East. The Hurricanes can see them now.

The August 20 briefing asked what Miami could do before Charlotte arrived. A sweep was worth four games, and the Hurricanes needed help to get close enough to take first. They dropped three of four in Atlanta, then beat Tampa Bay twice. They entered the Charlotte series farther back than they had been on August 19. Addie de Ruijter drove in all four Miami runs in the opener. The sweep put Miami half a game ahead of Chicago for the wild card.

In The Pennant Races Come Home, Big Earl backed Charlotte and looked to the Central for the NBC wild card. Charlotte still has the division lead. Miami’s four wins have put the second part of that forecast in doubt. The August 20 conversation was an editorial reconstruction. Its forecasts belong to that date and the standings now belong to August 30.
Dallas beat Detroit. Chicago kept coming.

Detroit opened the challenge one game back of Dallas. On August 21, Heriberto Jimenez struck out 13 in eight scoreless innings in Chicago’s 1–0 win. Chicago took three of the four from Detroit and drew level with Dallas by August 26. The finale the briefing circled, Detroit at Dallas, became four wins for the Rustlers. Anton Garay gave them eight scoreless innings in the 4–0 third game. Detroit scored four runs in the entire series and finished the challenge 1–9.

Big Earl favored Dallas or Detroit over Chicago. Dallas answered for itself. So did the Fire, who took three of four in Minneapolis and finished just one game behind. The Central has six more Dallas–Chicago games on the schedule, including the last four in Dallas. That is enough baseball for the order to change without waiting on anybody else.
The West was worth watching. Both of them were.

Phoenix and San Francisco started level. Phoenix took three games at San Francisco, including a 2–0 game in which Tony Zacate gave the Firebirds eight scoreless innings. The Warriors answered with three wins in four against Los Angeles. Phoenix finished one up on San Francisco and two up on Los Angeles. Earl’s forecast of a San Francisco recovery is still within reach. The first series gave the Firebirds some reason to believe in their own place.

Across the league, Seattle opened with three wins over Las Vegas. In the 14th inning on August 21, David Olguin stole second, took third on the throwing error and scored on Adam Wilson’s single. By August 29 the Comets and Gamblers shared first. Denver then took the last two games of its series in Seattle, 4–2 and 2–1, and Las Vegas closed with a win in Portland. Earl’s Las Vegas pick still sits first. His Denver wild-card pick now shares the line with Seattle. All three clubs will see one another again before the schedule runs out.
Houston still owns the margin

The briefing flagged the extra St. Louis–Houston game. The Stallions completed that 5–3 win and swept the four regular games in St. Louis. They went 9–2, the best record of the challenge, and drew even with Cincinnati. Houston went 3–8 and still leads both clubs by eight. The Mavericks have room to absorb a bad week. St. Louis has a reason to keep asking how much room there is.

Philadelphia won eight straight after two shutout losses in Boston. It picked up one game on the Patriots, whose final weekend included Jorge Galvez’s five-hit shutout in Pittsburgh. Houston and Boston both still sit atop their divisions. Las Vegas does, too. August gave Earl’s American Conference picks their places in the standings and gave the clubs behind them reasons to keep playing for those places.

Start September by watching who can take a series from a contender outside its own division. Miami opens at Phoenix and Detroit at San Francisco. The head-to-head games return later in September. The first job is to be close enough when they do.

portland-campbell-and-the-contenders.title: Jeremy Campbell gave the West something to work around
sections: Portland won three straight in Denver to open the challenge. Then it lost both games to Seattle, took two from Las Vegas and finished 5–5. Eighteen games out, the Lumberjacks still made each of the three West contenders account for them.

Jeremy Campbell hit seven homers and drove in 13 in those ten games. He went deep once in Portland’s 5–3 win against Las Vegas and twice in the 6–5 win the following day. Frank Jahr saved four games during the challenge without an earned run. The Lumberjacks had scoring and late innings worth following even when they could make little immediate use of the wins themselves.
St. Louis arrives just off a 9–2 stretch. Portland has a chance to find out whether Campbell’s August work carries into another series against a club with something at stake.

san-diego-what-two-wins-took.title: San Diego found a way to take two from first place
sections: The Seraphs had one run in the two middle games at Los Angeles and were swept, though the last loss took 14 innings. At home they beat San Francisco 4–3 and took consecutive games from Phoenix, 3–1 and 5–3. Those two wins took two days out of the Firebirds’ chance to extend their West lead.

Barbu Nica let in one earned run over 14⅓ innings in two starts during the challenge. Elijah Lundy gave the Seraphs 14⅔ innings and allowed three earned runs in his two. There is more to learn from those outings than from the club’s 48–83 record alone, especially when the offense supplied only 23 runs in ten games.

Minneapolis visits September 1. With roster expansion scheduled that day, the immediate question is how San Diego uses the innings around its starters, and whether the extra places turn into real work on the field.

san-francisco-foothold-against-los-angel.title: San Francisco found a foothold against Los Angeles
sections: The August 20 forecast called for a San Francisco recovery against familiar opponents. Phoenix took three of four in the Warriors’ own park. San Francisco then split two at San Diego. The recovery finally found a place to start in the four with Los Angeles, and the Warriors ended the challenge one game out instead of looking up at both rivals.

San Francisco put 15 runs on Los Angeles in the opener and won the last two. Bernardo Valenzuela homered and drove in three in the 10–4 finale. Miguel Collado hit four home runs over the full challenge. The offense that scored five runs in its last three games before the Los Angeles series scored 34 in the four against the Cobras.
Detroit comes to San Francisco on August 31. A Warriors win and a Phoenix loss would tie the West again. The next Phoenix series waits until September 28, also on the Warriors’ field.

seattle-what-a-one-run-game-costs.title: Seattle saw both sides of a one-run finish
sections: Adam Wilson singled in the 14th inning August 21, scoring David Olguin to beat Las Vegas 4–3. Seattle took three of four from the Gamblers and both games at Portland. It shared first before the final day. Then Denver won the finale 2–1, and Las Vegas finished its own trip with a win.

Tony Miller struck out eight in 7⅓ innings in that last loss. Carlos Merlos had 17 hits during the challenge. Seattle went 7–3 and made up four games on Las Vegas. Losing the last two let Denver catch it.

Nashville comes in on August 31. Denver and Seattle share the wild-card line at 71–60, and Las Vegas still has to come back to Seattle for three September 28–30. The Comets get time to get ahead before the next couple of one-run games carry the same kind of price.

st-louis-made-up-six-games.title: St. Louis made up six games and earned another look
sections: St. Louis won five games against Houston before the two clubs were done with their opening assignment. One was the completion of the unfinished game in Houston. The other four came at home. Chris Jorge threw a six-hit shutout in the 9–0 finale. Danny Martinez had seven hits over the two shutout wins that ended that set.

The Stallions won three of four from Cincinnati, too. In the 4–2 finale Bert Lopez struck out eight in 7⅔ innings. An 11-game challenge produced nine wins, 77 runs and the same 67–64 record as Cincinnati. St. Louis already has five more wins than it managed in all of 1980. It is eight behind Houston and four off the wild-card line.

The Stallions go to Portland on August 31. Houston visits again September 28–30, immediately after four at Cincinnati. That run will test whether the gains St. Louis made playing those clubs in August can survive the rest of its schedule.

tampa-bay-kimpton-kept-reaching.title: Tampa Bay kept finding Walter Kimpton on base
sections: Nate Smeltz drove in five on August 23, and the Storm needed them in a 10–9 win over Charlotte. It was the club’s only win of the challenge. Tampa Bay later took Atlanta to the 14th and lost 8–6. The two games are worth keeping separate from the 81 runs the Storm allowed across the ten-game stretch.

Walter Kimpton had 12 hits, ten walks and six stolen bases in the challenge. The Storm scored only four runs in two games at Miami and were shut out in their first game back home. Kimpton kept giving the batters behind him a chance to change that pattern.

The Storm go to Los Angeles next. With the expansion date approaching, keep Kimpton’s trips on base in view and watch which hitters get the chances to move him. There is a September job to define even with Tampa Bay 19 games out.
